summary: Comments from Abhay Bhushan on the File Transfer Protocol in RFC 354. They include corrections to errors in the text, extra discussion, points to stress and additions to the protocol. He says he will fold them into the main document after enough experience.

plainLanguage.summary: The author of the file-sharing rules lists mistakes and extra ideas to add. He will update the main rule book later.

questions: what are the ftp mlfl and mail commands
subtitle: Errata, clarifications and new commands for the 1972 File Transfer Protocol of RFC 354.

tldr.problem: RFC 354 contained typos, ambiguous wording, and gaps such as unclear print file types and no way to send mail or supply an account.
tldr.mechanism: Seventeen numbered comments fix errors, set a minimum server implementation, redefine print types, clarify data connection handling and add the MLFL, MAIL and ACCT commands.
tldr.outcome: The author planned to fold these comments into the main protocol document after enough experience. The RFC was later updated by RFC 414.

today: The unit metadata lists the status as unknown. This RFC updates RFC 354 and was itself updated by RFC 414.

sections.title: Corrections and Minimum Server
sections.content:
These comments update RFC 354. The first lists six small corrections, such as replacing user-FTP by server-FTP on page 2 and _CRCRLF_ by _CRLF_ on page 28.

The second comment says the word recommended for default parameters should be read as required. A server therefore needs at least: type ASCII (8-bit bytes), mode Stream, structure File, and the commands RETR, STOR, USER (and PASS), SOCK and BYE. Case does not matter in command syntax or in the symbols for type, mode and structure, so A and a both mean ASCII.
sections.plainLanguage: The author fixes spelling slips and says which parts are not optional: a basic file server must do at least these few things.

sections.title: Types, Modes and the Data Connection
sections.content:
The two print file types of RFC 354 are said to be incorrectly specified, because the real problem is ASA (Fortran) vertical format control. Three types are described instead, denoted E for EBCDIC, P for Print file-ASCII and F for formatted (ASA standard) EBCDIC print file. Under ASA control the first character of a record is not printed but sets spacing: blank for one line, 0 for two lines, 1 for the first line of the next page, and + for no advance.

Stream mode has the advantages that the receiver need not scan the bytes and that it works with all data types. Its disadvantages are that signalling end of file by closing the connection is not reliable, and that an end of record marked by CRLF is only valid if sender and receiver agree beforehand. In Block mode, unused left-most bits become "don't care" bits, and an end of file is an implicit end of record.

The user-FTP must listen on the data socket before sending a command that needs a transfer, and must not wait for the 255 reply. Any closing of the data connection should happen immediately after the transfer. A new reply, 454, means the server cannot connect to your data socket. Type supersedes Byte, so TYPE should be sent before BYTE.
sections.plainLanguage: The note explains how to mark the end of a page or a file, tells the receiving side to get its ears ready before the sender starts, and adds a new error message for when the connection cannot be made.

sections.title: New Commands: MLFL, MAIL and ACCT
sections.content:
MLFL (mail file) replaces using the append command for mail files. The user field can be empty, a NIC identifier or a system identifier, and the mail file travels over the data connection in ASCII type. Its success reply is 250 or 252, and failures use 451, 452, 453, 454 and 500-506.

MAIL sends mail over the Telnet connection instead, which is easier for TIP users. After the command the server treats following lines as the mail text until a line containing only a single period. New replies are 350 (enter mail) and 256 (mail completed).

ACCT carries an account specification for systems such as TENEX. Unlike PASS it may arrive at any time. Because passwords are sensitive, masking them is the user-FTP process's responsibility, since the server has no fool-proof way to do it. Experimental commands should begin with X, with any new reply codes chosen between 900 and 999.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new buttons are added: one to send a letter as a file, one to type a letter directly, and one to say which account to charge. Anyone may try out their own new buttons if the name starts with X.

references.text: NWG/RFC 189, cited for ASA vertical format control in its Appendix C.
